source_title: 1-year survival rates for new business establishments by year and location (The Economics Daily); Business Employment Dynamics survival data
publisher_issuer: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Business Employment Dynamics (BED) program
company_context: This is a government statistical source establishing base rates for business survival and failure, not a single company. The BLS Business Employment Dynamics (BED) program tracks establishment-level birth, survival, and death across cohorts. It provides the population-level priors against which any individual distressed-company diagnosis should be calibrated: most new businesses are NOT failing in any given year, but cumulative failure rises steadily over a decade.
business_type: Government statistical dataset - US private-sector business establishment survival/failure base rates (cross-industry)
evidence_summary: Per BLS Business Employment Dynamics data, about 22.1% of new US private-sector business establishments fail within their first year, meaning roughly 77.9% survive year one. Cumulative attrition rises over time: roughly half of new establishments close by about year five (reported around 48.6% closed by five years, i.e., ~51.4% surviving, with cohort-dependent estimates in the ~42-50% survival range), and after ten years about two-thirds (around 65.3%) are no longer operating. Survival varies by birth cohort and business cycle - establishments born into a recession generally show lower five-year survival than recovery-period cohorts. These base rates are the priors for distinguishing a genuinely distressed firm from one that is merely young, and for calibrating whether a given trajectory is anomalous versus typical.

source_backed_metrics.ten_year_closure_rate_pct: approximately 65.3% no longer operating after ten years
source_backed_metrics.data_program: BLS Business Employment Dynamics (BED) establishment survival series
source_backed_metrics.key_modifier: Survival rates vary by birth-year cohort and business cycle; recession-born cohorts have lower 5-year survival

outcome_evidence: Population-level base rates: ~77.9% one-year survival, roughly half surviving to five years, ~one-third surviving to ten years; outcome is 'stable healthy' for the majority in the near term, with rising attrition over a decade.
source_limitations: Source is a BLS Economics Daily summary of Business Employment Dynamics establishment-survival data on the primary government domain (bls.gov); direct WebFetch returned HTTP 403 in this environment, so percentages rely on verbatim search-result snippets attributed to BLS plus one corroborating secondary aggregation. The 22.1% one-year figure is also widely cited via secondary outlets citing BLS BED; exact cohort year should be confirmed against the specific BED release table for any quantitative use.
directly_stated: About 22.1% of new businesses fail within the first year
Roughly half of new establishments close by five years (~48.6%)
About 65.3% are no longer operating after ten years
Survival varies by cohort and business cycle (recession cohorts lower)
inferred: These rates serve as priors for judging whether an individual firm's distress is anomalous or typical for its age
Young-firm attrition should not be auto-labeled as a fixable intervention target without a firm-specific diagnosis
why_useful_for_opsiq: Provides authoritative base rates so OpsIQ can calibrate business-condition assessment and avoid over-diagnosing distress in young firms (anchoring the 'stable healthy' vs 'failure' priors). Useful as a public-dataset/government reference for the BusinessConditionProfile prior, and as a control for category-12 stable-healthy versus category-1 failure classification.
